headline: Ukraine hits Russian oil sites with drones

sources.title: Drone offensive hits Russian oil tankers and refineries at 'industrial scale' as Moscow bans diesel exports
Russia bans diesel exports after Ukrainian attacks, straining already tense global market
Russia Bans Diesel Exports to Ensure Domestic Supply After Targeted Ukrainian Drone Strikes
Ukraine hits Russia's largest refinery in one of its deepest strikes yet | DW News (video, DW News)

chunks.text: Ukraine {{carried out}} a large drone [[offensive]] that [[lasted]] about three days. Ukraine said its forces {{stepped up}} attacks on Russian oil [[tankers]] and [[refineries]]. One Ukrainian [[commander]] [[described]] the campaign as reaching an "industrial scale." [[According to reports]], the drones {{set off}} fires at several energy sites, and Ukraine [[claimed]] it had hit 21 [[vessels]], including 19 oil tankers, near Crimea.

verbs.wrong: To win a battle after long fighting
verbs.correct: To do or complete a planned task or action
verbs.why: Soldiers carry out orders, and a company carries out a survey of its workers. Ukraine carried out a drone offensive that lasted about three days and targeted Russian oil tankers and refineries.

verbs.wrong: To aim at more important targets
verbs.correct: To increase or intensify an activity
verbs.why: A gym steps up security after trouble, and factories step up production before the holidays. Ukraine's military stepped up its attacks on Russian oil tankers and refineries, calling the campaign industrial scale.

verbs.wrong: To destroy something in an explosion
verbs.correct: To cause something to start suddenly
verbs.why: A spark can set off an explosion, and a loud noise can set off a dog barking down the street. According to reports, Ukraine's drones set off fires at several Russian energy sites near Crimea.

chunks.text: The strikes {{knocked out}} part of Russia's oil [[production]]. According to reports, the Omsk refinery in Siberia, which is Russia's largest, {{shut down}} some [[operations]] after it was hit. The plant sits about 1,700 miles from Ukrainian [[territory]] and [[normally]] makes around 460,000 [[barrels]] of fuel a day. Two industry sources said work at the site stopped [[for a time]].

verbs.wrong: To reduce something to half its size
verbs.correct: To destroy or stop something from working
verbs.why: Heavy rain can knock out the internet for a whole neighborhood, and a power surge can knock out a computer in seconds. Ukraine's strikes knocked out a real share of Russia's oil production, at least for a while.

verbs.wrong: To move work to a safer place
verbs.why: An airport shuts down in thick fog, and a store shuts down for the holidays. Russia's largest refinery, in Siberia, shut down part of its operations after Ukrainian drones hit the site.

chunks.text: Inside Russia, the attacks [[led to]] serious fuel [[shortages]]. Long lines {{built up}} at gas stations in several regions, and some areas {{brought in}} [[limits on]] how much fuel drivers could buy. Prices {{went up}} quickly. One Russian official said the situation at filling stations was "[[causing concern]]" among the public, and reports said some stations {{ran out}} of gasoline.

verbs.wrong: To appear suddenly all at once
verbs.correct: To increase or grow larger gradually
verbs.why: Traffic builds up during rush hour, and debt can build up quietly over many years. Long lines built up at gas stations across several Russian regions as the fuel shortage spread.

verbs.wrong: To ask people to follow a rule voluntarily
verbs.correct: To introduce a new rule, law, or system
verbs.why: A school brings in stricter rules, and a city brings in a ban on plastic bags. Several Russian regions brought in limits on how much fuel each driver could buy during the shortage.

verbs.wrong: To change many times in one day
verbs.correct: To rise or increase in level or amount
verbs.why: Ticket prices go up right before a big show sells out, and rent goes up a little every year. Across Russia, fuel prices went up quickly as the shortage at gas stations spread.

verbs.wrong: To close early for the day
verbs.correct: To have no more of something left
verbs.why: A car runs out of gas on the highway, and a printer runs out of paper in the middle of a meeting. During the shortage, some Russian gas stations simply ran out of gasoline to sell.

chunks.text: [[In response]], Russia {{hit back}} at the [[pressure]] on its fuel market by cutting [[exports]]. Russian officials said they would {{hold back}} [[diesel]] exports until July 31 to keep enough fuel at home. To {{deal with}} the shortages, reports said Russia planned to buy fuel from other countries and had already started [[importing]] gasoline from India. [[Analysts]] said the export [[ban]] could push global diesel prices higher.

verbs.wrong: To protect your economy from losses
verbs.correct: To respond to an attack or criticism
verbs.why: A mayor hits back at critics during a press conference, and a company sometimes hits back at false claims. Russia hit back at the pressure on its fuel market by cutting diesel exports for weeks.

verbs.wrong: To increase the tax rate on diesel fuel
verbs.correct: To keep or stop something from being released
verbs.why: You might hold back your opinion at a meeting, and a dam holds back millions of gallons of water. Russian officials said they would hold back diesel exports until July 31 to protect the home fuel supply.

verbs.wrong: To limit how much fuel drivers could buy
verbs.correct: To take action to solve a problem
verbs.why: A plumber has to deal with a broken pipe fast, and managers deal with customer complaints every day. To deal with its fuel shortage, Russia began buying gasoline from other countries, including India.

mainIdea.s: Ukraine launched a drone offensive that hit Russian oil tankers and refineries over three days. The strikes caused fuel shortages, so Russia banned diesel exports.
mainIdea.why: Ukraine's drones knocked out part of Russia's oil production, and Russia banned diesel exports until July 31 to keep fuel at home.

mainIdea.s: Ukraine's drones hit Russian oil sites in a three-day offensive against refineries and tankers. Russia then raised diesel exports to profit from higher world fuel prices.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Russia banned diesel exports to keep fuel at home, not raised them for profit. Officials said they would hold back exports until July 31.

mainIdea.s: Ukrainian and Russian officials held a new round of peace talks last month but again failed to agree on a ceasefire deal. Officials said the talks would continue.
mainIdea.why: This describes peace talks between the two countries. The article is about drone strikes on oil sites and fuel shortages.

tf.s: Ukraine carried out a large drone offensive that lasted about three days.
tf.why: Ukraine carried out (did) the planned offensive. This matches what happened.

tf.s: As fuel became hard to find, prices went down across Russia.
tf.why: Prices went up (rose) during the shortage. Go down means to fall, which is the opposite of what happened.

tf.s: To deal with the shortages, Russia planned to buy fuel from other countries.
tf.why: Russia moved to deal with (handle) the shortages by importing fuel. This is correct.

tf.s: Inside Russia, some gas stations ran out of gasoline during the shortages.
tf.why: The stations ran out (had none left) of gasoline. This matches the reports.

tf.s: Ukraine called off its attacks on Russian oil tankers and refineries.
tf.why: Ukraine stepped up (increased) its attacks. Call off means to cancel, which is not what happened.

tf.s: Russia stepped up its diesel exports until the end of July.
tf.why: Russia held back (stopped) its diesel exports. Step up means to increase, which is the opposite of what happened.
